question: Why does boosting work, how is it equivalent to forward stagewise additive modelling, and how does gradient tree boosting with shrinkage, subsampling and right-sized trees yield an accurate off-the-shelf learner?
hypothesis: Boosting is fitting an additive model in tree basis functions by stagewise optimisation of a loss; robust differentiable losses plus slow learning make it an effective data-mining procedure.
contributions: AdaBoost fits an additive model under exponential loss (Sec 10.2-10.4)
Population minimizer of exponential loss is half the log-odds (Sec 10.5)
Robust losses for regression and classification (Sec 10.6)
Gradient boosted models for any differentiable loss (Sec 10.10)
Relative importance and partial dependence for interpretation (Sec 10.13)

limits: Chapter is a textbook exposition: simulation and application results come with few settings (M, nu and eta often not stated; gbm settings only partly given).
Authors concede boosting sacrifices speed, interpretability and (for AdaBoost) robustness to overlapping classes and mislabelling relative to single trees (Sec 10.7).
Theory bounds for AdaBoost are 'too loose to be of practical importance' (Bibliographic Notes); debate about why boosting works continues (Mease and Wyner 2008 vs Friedman et al. 2008a).

Pre-2009: covers MART/gbm/mboost/TreeNet; no XGBoost, LightGBM, second-order (Newton) tree boosting, histogram splits, or explicit tree-complexity penalties. Only single-step Newton for multiclass (Ex. 10.8).
Partial dependence assumes inputs not strongly interacting with the complement; marginal average differs from conditional expectation (Sec 10.13.2).
practices: Use gradient tree boosting rather than plain AdaBoost for data mining; it keeps most advantages of trees (mixed types, missing values, monotone-transformation invariance) and loses speed and interpretability (Sec 10.7, p. 352).
Restrict all trees to the same size J treated as a meta-parameter; 4 <= J <= 8 works well, J about 6 is rarely beaten, J>10 unlikely needed (Sec 10.11, p. 363).
Set J to the dominant interaction order of the target plus one; J=2 gives a purely additive model (Sec 10.11, p. 362).
Use a small learning rate nu < 0.1 and choose number of iterations M by early stopping on a validation sample (Sec 10.12, pp. 364-365).
Use stochastic gradient boosting with subsample fraction eta about 1/2 (smaller for large N) (Sec 10.12.2, p. 365).
Explore J, nu and eta first and leave M as the main tuning parameter (p. 367).
Use binomial/multinomial deviance rather than exponential loss when label noise or probability estimates matter (Sec 10.6, pp. 347-349).
Use absolute or Huber loss for regression with outliers or long tails; Huber delta_m is the alpha-th quantile of |y - f| (Sec 10.6, Table 10.2).
Fit trees to negative gradients (pseudo-residuals) by least squares, then set leaf constants by a separate line search (Algorithm 10.3, p. 361).
Interpret fitted boosted models with relative variable importance (largest scaled to 100) and low-dimensional partial dependence plots (Sec 10.13, pp. 367-370).
Use 10-fold CV to choose number of terms and shrinkage (NZ fish example, p. 376).
Pick the number of iterations less carefully for large data with shrinkage: test error flattens and overfitting is mild (California housing, p. 371).

terms.definition: one whose error rate is only slightly better than random guessing
sequentially fits classifiers on reweighted data and combines them by weighted majority vote G(x)=sign(sum alpha_m G_m(x))
sequentially adding new basis functions to the expansion without adjusting the parameters and coefficients of those that have already been added
L(y,f(x)) = exp(-y f(x)); population minimizer is half the log-odds of P(Y=1|x)
y f(x); positive means correctly classified
squared error for |y-f| <= delta, 2 delta |y-f| - delta^2 otherwise
fit a regression tree to the negative gradient (pseudo-residuals) at each step; MART = multiple additive regression trees
components of the negative gradient r_im = -dL(y_i,f(x_i))/df(x_i) at f=f_{m-1}
scale each tree's contribution by 0 < nu < 1: f_m = f_{m-1} + nu * sum_j gamma_jm I(x in R_jm)
at each iteration sample a fraction eta of the training observations without replacement and grow the next tree on the subsample
sum over internal nodes of squared improvement for splits on the variable, averaged over trees; sqrt taken and largest scaled to 100
marginal average f_S(X_S)=E_{X_C} f(X_S,X_C), estimated by averaging over training values of X_C

code.snippet: AdaBoost.M1: w_i=1/N; for m=1..M: fit G_m with weights w_i; err_m = sum w_i I(y_i != G_m(x_i)) / sum w_i; alpha_m = log((1-err_m)/err_m); w_i <- w_i exp[alpha_m I(y_i != G_m(x_i))]; output G(x)=sign[sum alpha_m G_m(x)]

Gradient tree boosting: f_0(x)=argmin_gamma sum L(y_i,gamma); for m=1..M: (a) r_im = -[dL(y_i,f(x_i))/df(x_i)]_{f=f_{m-1}}; (b) fit regression tree to r_im giving regions R_jm; (c) gamma_jm = argmin_gamma sum_{x_i in R_jm} L(y_i, f_{m-1}(x_i)+gamma); (d) f_m(x)=f_{m-1}(x)+sum_j gamma_jm I(x in R_jm)
f_m(x) = f_{m-1}(x) + nu * sum_{j=1}^{J} gamma_jm I(x in R_jm)
K-class: p_k(x)=exp f_k/sum exp f_l; r_ikm = y_ik - p_k(x_i); fit tree to r_ikm; gamma_jkm = ((K-1)/K) sum r_ikm / sum |r_ikm|(1-|r_ikm|); f_km = f_k,m-1 + sum_j gamma_jkm I(x in R_jkm)
